# Cold Email Frameworks — Real Experts Series (Expert Interviews) v2
<!-- verify-allow: ai -->

**What changed from v1:** The reply reward is now the three interview questions written only for them, in every framework close (Strategist pillar 4). Every close also carries an easy out from a bank of ten or more, and no close or out repeats within a lead. Openers vary: at most 3 of the 13 relevance lines start with "Saw", and no two frameworks in a row open with the same verb. Each follow-up has a named job, never opens with "following up on", and only the F1, F4, F7 and F10 follow-ups carry the page link. Every framework gets a spin set (subject with 3+ options, greeting, sign-off). The terms line is rewritten so it is no longer a three-item list, and "no charge" appears once per lead, in F3 only. F8's credibility line is now "I've taught 300 agency owners, and I was asked to speak at an AI summit." The list is filtered on the review pattern before research starts. New in v2: the close bank, the escape-hatch bank, the closer opt-out bank, the follow-up job table, the spintax rules, the attack plan, the infrastructure checklist and the weekly rhythm.

**Purpose:** 10 frameworks, each with its own follow-up, plus 3 alternates and two closers (22 touches per lead), built for an AI agent to research and write per lead. The goal of every email is one thing: a reply. Not a booking, not a click. The reply gets the lead three questions, written only for them, with the page and the calendar under them, and the setter takes it from there.

**What we're inviting them to:** the Real Experts Series. A 20 to 30 minute recorded interview with people who are genuinely the best at what they do, about what they've learned. We send it to our email list and feature it on our socials. After that it's theirs to share. It isn't a pitch, and nothing is hidden.

**The thesis (the reason the series exists):** no matter how good AI gets, it can't replace the wisdom of an industry veteran. It isn't intelligence or textbook knowledge. It's the experience, the intuition, the instincts and the unspoken understandings that only come from doing the work for years.

**The signature image: the ninety seconds.** The mechanic who hears the car pull into the lot and knows it's the timing belt before the driver gets out. The bookkeeper who looks at a P&L for ninety seconds and asks the question three accountants missed. Every real expert has a moment like this, where they know in seconds what took twenty years to learn. Nobody has ever asked them how they know. Every framework echoes this moment in that lead's own field.

**The spine (in every email, and it is true):** the internet is filling up with answers from things that have never done the job, and from people with a ring light and two years in. The people who actually know are the quietest ones online, because they're busy doing the work. What they know isn't on the record anywhere. We want to put it there.

**Naming mode:** branded. "The Real Experts Series" (or "Real Experts Series") appears once per framework email, in the offer sentence, matter-of-factly. Never in a subject line. Never twice in one email. No other company names, ours or anyone's. The sending domain and the page link come out in four follow-ups (F1, F4, F7, F10) and on reply.

**Close type:** walkthrough, reply-triggered. One decision per email: reply. The reward is the three questions, written only for them from research, sent the same day. Every close pairs the ask with a plain way out. F10 ends on a soft question instead, with its own short out folded in just before the question.

**Tracks:**
- **Track A (default): the quiet expert.** No podcast, no YouTube channel, no regular posting. What they know lives in their head and in their reviews.
- **Track B: the expert who already talks.** They have a podcast, a YouTube channel, a newsletter, or post regularly about their work. Same series, different opening: you already share it, here's a new room of people who should hear it. Track B leads with Alternate A and gets the Track B variant of Closer 2.

**Niche:** experts in every field, US. Anyone who is the person other people in their field call when they're stuck: auto and repair, home and trades, personal care, health and wellness, family and pets, food and hospitality, real estate and property, professional services, marketing and creative, technology, product founders, coaching and consulting. The segment swap table carries the language for each.

**Positioning:** an interview series, not a podcast pitch, not an agency, not a pay-to-be-featured outlet. Most "we'd love to feature you" emails these people get are a sales pitch in a costume. This one is the opposite, and every email proves it with the terms line.

**Sender:** `{sender}`, the first name on the inbox that is actually sending. First person "I." See the sender roster below.

**THE SENDER ROSTER (read before writing a single email):**

| Flag | What it controls | If false |
|---|---|---|
| `hosts_the_interviews` | Whether this sender personally does the interviews | Every first-person host line swaps to Justin. "I'd interview you" becomes "Justin, who hosts it, would interview you." "The three questions I'd ask you" becomes "the three questions Justin would ask you." "I only record..." becomes "Justin only records...". Every example with a first-person host line carries a one-line `Roster false:` swap under it. Never claimed by someone who doesn't host. |
| `justin_background` | Whether the sender is Justin (the credibility line is his) | F8 uses the third person: "Justin, who runs it, has taught 300 agency owners and was asked to speak at an AI summit." Or the inbox skips F8. No inbox borrows Justin's background in the first person. |

Missing roster means both flags are false.

**Word count:** framework emails 85 to 100 words, counting greeting and sign-off. Follow-ups 30 to 50, one question at the end. Closer 1 under 50. Closer 2 under 100.

**Tone:** plain text. Lowercase subjects. Peer to peer, warm, curious, a little in awe of what they know. The reader should feel seen, not sold. If a sentence would fit on a marketing page, cut it. If it sounds like a keynote, rewrite it until it sounds like a voicemail. Reading grade 5 is the target, grade 7 the ceiling.

**Campaign structure:** the Sept 3, 2026 house policy. 10 framework emails + 10 follow-ups + 2 closers per lead. See the Campaign Structure section.

## §0 ATTACK PLAN — HOW WE ATTACK

**Verdict header**
- `OFFER: GO (7/10 with fixes 1 and 2 adopted; 8/10 pending Open Item 7a)`
- `MODE: Standard 22-touch. No Sprint. Spearhead tier off until the referral-partner priority list exists.`
- `FREE THING: three interview questions written only for them, from research, sent the same day they reply`

**What this means, in one paragraph.** The v1 copy is strong, and copy cannot rescue an offer. From the prospect's side, the v1 offer is a respectful invitation with no proof behind it and a reply reward ("more info") that is not worth anything on its own. Two fixes, both inside the doc's own bans, take it to 7/10, GO: make the three questions the default reply reward, and filter the list on the review pattern before research starts. v2 adopts both. A third fix needs facts confirmed first (Open Items 7a and 7b): name the edited interview and clips as an asset they keep, which makes it 8/10 (see 3c, not live until then). Proof stays at 0 until real interviews exist. We do not invent it. The real business goal, referral partnerships, sits behind the curtain. So the number that matters is not interviews recorded but referral conversations started, and the plan below measures it.

### 1. Target

- **Who:** the named expert in a US business, meaning the person customers ask for by name. In a firm, that is the partner or principal who is the expert, not the marketing person. In a family business, it is whoever the reviews name. There are 12 segments, per the swap table: auto and repair, home and trades, personal care, health and wellness, family/pets/learning, food and hospitality, real estate and property, professional services, marketing and creative, technology, product founders, coaching and consulting.
- **Hard filters (at list build, before research):**
  1. A person is named in the reviews or on the site as the practitioner. Faceless brands and franchise locations with no named expert are out.
  2. The review-pattern signal is present (see 2).
  3. A personal or named-person email address can be found and verified. If the only address is a generic inbox, the lead goes to a lower-priority pool and is not dropped.
  4. Not already a contact, a past guest or a referral partner. The do-not-contact list is checked.
- **Filters that stay per lead (already in the doc):** at least 2 Gold or Silver details or the lead is skipped (the routing rule), the Track A/B check, and the regulated-field check.
- **Segment priority at launch:** `[NEEDS: which segments the referral-partnership business most wants as partners]`. The interview is the front door to that business, so the list should lean toward the segments the back end serves. Until Justin answers, weight toward segments where reviews name a person and a judgment skill (auto and repair, home and trades, personal care, family and pets). Those have the densest Gold details and the lowest regulatory exposure. Track B segments (marketing, technology, coaching) run on Alt A.
- **TAM:** no count yet. `[NEEDS: TAM count]`. Method:
  1. Pull Google Maps listings by segment category and by metro through `lead-warehouse` and `apify-enrich`.
  2. Hand-check a random sample per segment against hard filters 1 to 3, and record the pass rate.
  3. TAM per segment = listings pulled × measured pass rate. Report it by segment, with the sample size beside it.

  Professional services and regulated fields can also be pulled from license boards and association directories.

### 2. Signals

- **The signal: the review pattern.** Customers have written down the expert's ninety seconds themselves. Several reviews name the same judgment skill: found what others missed, knew right away, talked me out of the thing I didn't need, the one other pros call. This is what makes the invitation feel earned rather than mass-sent, and it is the list-level version of the doc's Gold detail.
- **Why it matters for the offer:** "every field, US" is a population, not a list. A list filtered on the review pattern puts the reason we're writing in the lead framework's relevance line (F1 by default), and turns a broadcast into "they actually looked." Details are never reused, so later emails open on further distinct review details or other Gold and Silver details, never the same one twice.
- **Secondary signals (route the sequence, not the list):** teaching, mentoring or hiring juniors (F10 moves forward), a family business or origin story (F5 leads), a visible FAQ or repeated customer question (F6 leads), Track B channels (Alt A leads), and no camera signals (Alt C).
- **Timeliness:** the thesis is timeless on purpose, and we do not manufacture a "why now." A milestone the expert posted themself (an anniversary year in business, an award, a new location) is a valid Silver detail when research finds one.
- **How List & Signals gets it in-house (no paid enrichment SaaS):**
  - Scrape Maps reviews with `apify-enrich` / Apify.
  - Score the review text against a phrase set for judgment skills, using an in-house AI pass. List & Signals writes the phrase set per segment and keeps the pass rate. We don't invent thresholds here.
  - Pull sites and about pages with `firecrawl` / browser-use.
  - Run the Track B check by searching YouTube and podcasts with browser-use.
  - Find emails by guessing the common patterns, then verify every address with `verify-emails` / `verify-leads` (self-hosted Reacher). Catch-all domains get catch-all verification.
  - Store everything in `lead-warehouse`.

### 3. Offer score: the 5 cold-traffic pillars, from the prospect's side

**3a. The offer as v1 states it:** a 20 to 30 minute recorded interview about what you've learned. We send it to our list and socials, and it's yours to share. No charge, no pitch, nothing hidden. Reply and I'll send more info.

| # | Pillar | Score | Evidence (one line) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Makes them money, reframed as being found by people who need them | **1** | The only allowed line is "if somebody watching needs what you do, they'll know where to find you." We can't state the list size, views or clients, so the visibility is real but unsized. "Theirs to share" is the one tangible asset. |
| 2 | Signal paired with the list | **1** | The list is "experts in every field, US." Per-lead research skips weak leads, but that filters after the pull. It is not a signal the list is built on. |
| 3 | Look-alike proof | **0** | No episodes, no guests, and the doc rightly bans "our last guest." F8's credibility line (300 agency owners, an AI summit) is proof about the sender, not look-alike proof. |
| 4 | Easy yes | **1** | The ask is tiny (a reply). But in 8 of 10 frameworks the reward is "more info," the page, which is not worth anything on its own. The reward that is (the three questions) appears in only 2 of 22 touches, F9 and Closer 2. Behind the reply sits a 45-minute on-camera call with a stranger. |
| 5 | Not Google-able | **2** | Nobody can search their way into being interviewed about their own judgment. One caveat: the three questions alone could be machine-written, so they are worth something only if they are built from a Gold detail. |
| | **Total** | **5/10** | Under 6, so **FIX FIRST**. No 0 on pillar 1 or 4. |

**3b. The fixes (each inside the doc's bans: no money talk, no "free" hook, no clients, no list size, no views):**

- **Pillar 4, from 1 to 2: make the reward valuable on its own.** The default reply reward in every framework becomes "the three questions I'd ask you, plus how it works." The three questions are already logged at research time (research item 10), so they go out the same day. F9 and Closer 2 keep their framing. Every other framework's close shifts from "reply for more" to "reply and I'll send the questions I'd ask you." The variation bank gets reworded to match, and the closes still never repeat within a lead. The reply templates already have the three-questions message. It becomes the default reply, with the page link under it.
- **Pillar 2, from 1 to 2: filter the list on the review pattern** (section 2) before research. Every lead then arrives with the reason we're writing already in hand.
- **Pillar 1, from 1 to 2 (conditional): name the asset, and name who will see it.**
  - First, the asset. The offer block and the feature line say they keep the edited interview and the short clips. Those clips can go on their site and profile, and to every customer who asks the question they answer fifty times (F6). The clips are what they'd otherwise hire a videographer and editor to make. We say the asset, never a price. `[NEEDS: confirm the full interview and clips are delivered as files they own, not only a link]`. If they only get a link, this pillar stays at 1.
  - Second, who sees it (pending Open Item 7b, never in live copy until confirmed). Add the honest version of the room line: the experts in the fields next to theirs see it too. These are the people who serve their customers before and after them. It promises no clients, and it is the true shape of what the series does.
- **Pillar 3 stays 0, and we say so.** It is fixed by a milestone, not by copy:
  1. Record the first interviews from Justin's warm network before the cold launch, or in parallel with it.
  2. Once guests approve and their interview is published, add a true look-alike line by segment, such as "I just recorded one with a {segment} in {state}." Name the guest only with their consent.

  Until then, the doc does what the playbook prescribes when there is no proof: lead with the terms and the free thing.

**3c. The rewritten offer (the 8/10 version). NOT LIVE until Open Items 7a and 7b are confirmed.** Until then the live text is the Offer Block, which leaves out both unconfirmed claims.
> A 20 to 30 minute recorded interview about what you've learned. Our team edits it and cuts short clips. You see it first, and once you approve it, the interview and the clips are yours to use anywhere. We share it with our list, our socials, and the experts in the fields around yours. No charge, no pitch, nothing hidden. Reply and I'll send you the three questions I'd ask you, and how it works.

The rewrite scores 2 + 2 + 0 + 2 + 2 = **8/10, GO**, once Open Items 7a and 7b are confirmed. Without them, the live copy scores 7/10 (fixes 1 and 2 adopted), which is still GO.

**3d. What this means for the business behind the curtain.** The prospect scores what they see: the interview. The business scores what comes after: a referral-partnership conversation that the prospect starts. Those are two different funnels joined by one call. The offer can score well and still produce nothing for the business, if interviews never turn into partnership conversations. That is why the testing plan (section 8) tracks the whole chain, and why the segment mix (section 1) needs Justin's answer on which partners the back end wants.

### 4. The free thing

- **What it is:** three interview questions written only for this expert. They come from their Gold and Silver details, their ninety seconds and their story hooks (research items 4 to 6). They are theirs whether they do the interview or not.
- **Why it qualifies (honestly):** it is in the house idea bank for interview offers ("Interviews, three questions written just for them"). Its value is that it proves somebody read their reviews and understood the work. It is weaker against the "give away what others charge for" rule, because people rarely pay for interview questions. So the questions must be specific enough that no other expert in the category could receive them. QC fails any question that passes the swap test (could it be sent to another business in their category?).
- **Same-day fulfilment:** the questions are written and logged at research time, before touch 1 goes out, so the reply goes back within minutes with no new research. The setter pastes them from the research log.
- **Held in reserve for the recycle:** a one-page "what your customers say you do that nobody else does" digest. It is built from the 20 or more reviews we already read, and it is worth having on its own. Marketers sell this kind of customer-voice summary. It needs no new data. For health and wellness, it quotes no outcomes or results.

### 5. Proof on file

- **True today, sender proof only:** Justin taught referral partnerships to 300 agency owners and was asked to speak at an AI summit. This line appears in F8 only, in the first person only when the sender is Justin.
- **Look-alike proof:** none. That stays true until real interviews are recorded, approved and published.
- **May NOT be claimed:** list size, audience size, views, reach, past guests, past episodes, "our last guest," any named guest, clients or new business for them, "we'll pay you" (parked, open item 1), any statistic about AI or the internet, and "a couple a day" until the recording schedule is confirmed (open item 2).

### 6. Campaign mode

- **Standard 22-touch (the default), as the doc's policy section states.** It is relationship-led, the ask is personal (their judgment, on the record), and the back-end goal is a partnership. All of these reward patience and many angles over speed.
- **No Sprint.** Sprint needs a strong offer and a fast-close motion. This offer is not strong until the fixes land, and a booking cadence pushing hard toward a call would contradict "no pitch, nothing hidden."
- **Spearhead tier: off at launch.** It turns on when two things exist: (a) Justin's list of the businesses he most wants as referral partners, and (b) at least one published interview to point to. The special thing for that tier is a printed card with their three questions, mailed before touch 1, followed by an email that names it.

### 7. Capacity math `[NEEDS: capacity]`

House constants: about 30 cold sends per inbox per day, 3 inboxes per domain (90 a day per domain, under the 100 cap), and +50% insurance inboxes warming on the side. Standard load is 22 touches per lead, so new leads a day = sends a day ÷ 22.

| Daily cold sends | Live inboxes | Live domains | Insurance inboxes | Insurance domains | Total inboxes / domains | New leads a day |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 34 (1,000 ÷ 30, rounded up) | 12 | 17 | 6 | 51 / 18 | about 45 |
| 3,000 | 100 | 34 | 50 | 17 | 150 / 51 | about 136 |

- **Steady state only:** sends = new leads × 22 holds only once every step of the sequence has cohorts in flight. Before that, the same new-lead rate sends less. The inbox count is the ceiling, not the starting volume.
- **Research load:** every new lead needs the full research checklist, plus the three questions, before touch 1. That means about 45 or about 136 fully researched leads a day, and research throughput is a constraint in its own right.
- **The likely binding constraint is the host's calendar, not the inboxes.** Open item 2 says Justin records about two interviews a day, and F7's scarcity line depends on that. Size the send volume from the recording ceiling:
  > sends a day needed = interviews a day ÷ (positive reply rate × book rate × show rate)

  All three rates are `[NEEDS: measured]`. We don't guess them. Once the first 1,000-send verdict produces real rates, solve this formula. If it calls for fewer sends than the inbox capacity, the extra inboxes go to the always-warm inventory instead of to more volume. If more people book than the host can record, either the roster adds a host (`hosts_the_interviews`), or F7's line changes and the volume comes down.

### 8. Testing plan

- **What counts as a positive for this offer:** a reply that asks for the questions, the info or the page, says yes or sure, answers the follow-up's question with real engagement, or asks the catch question in good faith. These do not count: not now, not interested, unsubscribe, auto-replies, and "is this a podcast" with no further interest.
- **First test (one variable):** how the reward is named in the closes. Both variants are the fixed offer, and both name the three questions as the reward. The unfixed v1 offer ("reply and I'll send more info") is never sent. The lead framework changes per lead, so it can't be the test variable.
  - **Variant A, the interview framing:** the closes name the reward as the questions the host would ask them ("the three questions I'd ask you").
  - **Variant B, the gift framing:** the closes name the reward as written only for them and theirs either way ("three questions written only for you").

  Both variants use the same list (the review-pattern filtered list), the same frameworks, the same close skeletons and outs, and the same inboxes. Only the reward phrase inside each close changes, and every close is still worded fresh.
- **Verdict thresholds:** no verdict before 1,000 sends per variant.
  - 1,000 sends and 0 positives: kill the variant, and change the offer or the list, not the subject.
  - 1,000 sends and 1 positive: scale to 3,000 before judging.
  - Count every touch, and attribute each positive to the step that produced it.
- **The full chain, tracked per lead:** positive, then booked, showed, recorded, approved, published, and finally a referral-partnership conversation that the guest starts (they asked how we make money, or asked about the work). The last link is the business metric. If interviews are recorded but no partnership conversations start, the series is working and the business is not. Fix that on the page and in the post-interview flow, never in the cold email.
- **Read by segment:** positives, bookings and partnership conversations by segment. The list moves toward the segments that do well on both the prospect side and the business side.
- **Next tests, in order and one at a time:** Track B (Alt A) as the lead framework against F1 for loud-segment leads, the subject set, and naming mode (branded against unbranded).
- **Who reads the results:** the Analyst, on the weekly rhythm. Results go into the campaign's results note in the Obsidian vault (booked, showed, recorded, partnership conversation), together with the next test chosen.

### 9. Reply plan

- **Who answers:** the reply-setter agent drafts, and Justin approves sends unless an auto-send policy is set for this campaign. Any reply pauses the sequence.
- **Speed:** within minutes, not hours. The three questions and the page are pre-built per lead, so there is nothing to research at reply time.
- **What goes back:** the three questions, then the page link with the lead's ref (`experts.truerevenuepartnerships.com/?ref={lead_ref}`), using the doc's reply templates.
- **Calendar:** the Expert Series event, about 45 minutes (15 to get acquainted, then the 20 to 30 minute interview, then the review booking). `[NEEDS: switch cal.com from the 30-minute discovery event to the Expert Series event]` (open item 3). Offer as many slots as the host's recording ceiling allows. The ceiling sets the slots, and the slots set the volume (section 7).
- **Caller hand-off:** none by default. A phone push contradicts the terms. Exception: a lead who replied positively and has a number but didn't book can get one warm call or text from the host. Then stop, and set the recycle trigger.
- **The catch question:** answer it with the doc's "how do you make money" reply, word for word in spirit. The referral-partnership work is said plainly and is never pitched on the call.

### 10. Trust readiness

- **Sender profile:** prospects will check who is asking. Justin's LinkedIn should show the series (a featured link to the page, and posts about what experts teach him once interviews exist). Every sending inbox needs a real first name, a Google profile photo and roster flags filled in (open item 5).
- **The page:**
  - Rename it to "Real Experts Series" (open item 6).
  - Replace "video coming soon" before the reply templates go live (open item 4).
  - Add one plain line saying who runs the series and what else they do. This makes "nothing hidden" literally true when someone checks.
- **Domains:** sending domains are lookalikes of the brand that owns the page, lead to a real site, and pass the pre-launch infrastructure gate. No inbox goes live until warmup health reads 99 to 100%.
- **Links:** none in framework emails, and one in follow-ups (the page with the ref). Turn off open tracking, or use a custom tracking domain.

### 11. Recycle plan

- **Trigger:** step 22 sent, no reply, plus the house recycle gap (reply-playbook §6). We never recycle a no, an unsubscribe or a rude reply.
- **What changes:** a new angle and a new free thing.
  - **New angle:** proof-led, once real published interviews exist in their segment ("I just recorded one with a {segment} in {state}").
  - **New free thing:** the review digest (section 4).
  - If no published interview exists in their segment when the trigger fires, the lead waits for one rather than recycling with the same angle.

### 12. Risks and open items

**Risks**

1. **The offer was FIX FIRST as v1 stated it (5/10).** v2 applies the two 3b fixes (the three questions as the reward in every close, and the review-pattern list filter), which makes it 7/10, GO. Pillar 1 rises to 2 (8/10) only once Open Item 7a is confirmed. 3c stays not live until 7a and 7b are confirmed.
2. **No look-alike proof.** Reply rates may be lower until real interviews exist. Mitigation: record warm-network interviews first, and lead with the terms and the questions.
3. **"Nothing hidden" against the business goal.** The terms line stays true only if three things hold: the interview call never pivots to a pitch, the referral-partnership talk happens only when the guest asks, and the page says plainly who runs it. If the setter or host ever pitches on the call, every email in this doc becomes the "pitch in a costume" it warns about (pain #10).
4. **Vanity-metric risk.** Interviews recorded are not the goal. If partnership conversations don't follow, fix the post-interview flow, not the cold email.
5. **Recording capacity.** If bookings outrun the host's calendar, the experience breaks and F7's scarcity line goes stale. Size volume to the calendar (section 7).
6. **The niche is broad.** Twelve segments in one campaign will hide which ones work. Read every number by segment.
7. **Regulated fields** (health, legal, finance, insurance, real estate licensing): no outcomes and no advice language, in email or in the interview edit.
8. **Generic inboxes.** Local businesses often show only info@ addresses. Writing to a named expert through a shared inbox weakens the relevance line. Those leads go in a lower-priority pool.
9. **The three questions read as generic.** If they could be sent to anyone in the category, the free thing is worthless and contradicts the thesis. QC enforces the swap test.

## THE CLAIMS SECTION — WHAT WE LEAN ON

This doc leans on an idea, not on news or statistics, so there are no numbers anywhere.

- **What's true and allowed:** a lot of what's online now is written by AI or by people with very little experience. Real experts tend to be busy doing the work and quiet online. Wisdom from experience is hard to write down and easy to lose.
- **Banned:** any percentage, count or study about AI content ("half the internet is AI," "90% of articles"). "Most" about online content (use "a lot of"). Any claim that AI is bad, dangerous or coming for their job. Any prediction. We celebrate the expert. We never attack the technology or scare the reader.
- **The word AI:** allowed ONLY as the thesis, in its designated frameworks (F2, F10, Alternate A) and in the "tell me more" reply, plus the words "an AI summit" inside the credibility line in F8. Once per email. Never about us, our tools, or how we do anything.
- **"Top 1%":** a description of who we're looking for, allowed once in a lead's whole sequence, never as a stat about them.
- **Freshness rule:** none needed. If a major AI news story breaks, do not hook onto it. The thesis is timeless on purpose.

## COLD EMAIL BEST PRACTICES — RULES FOR EVERY FRAMEWORK

**Subject lines:** 1 to 4 words, lowercase, vague, never selling, never the series name. Should look like a peer sent it. Every framework carries 3 or more options, spun in its spin set. Never "free", never "quick question" or "quick one", no fake "re:" or "fwd:", no stubs that read as a fragment ("your post on").

**Body structure (the four variables, in order):**
1. **Relevance:** one sentence, in the first two lines, carrying the one specific detail from research. It must pass the specificity test (see Research). Vary how it opens (see the opener rule below).
2. **The moment:** ONE pain from the ammo bank, written as their field's version of the ninety seconds or the truth around it. Never stack two.
3. **The invitation:** the Real Experts Series, what it is, carrying two or three signature lines at most.
4. **The close:** the reply ask with the three questions as the reward, worded fresh every time, plus one easy out.

**The close (reply is the trigger):**
- One decision in the email: reply. No links in framework emails, ever.
- **The reward is the three questions,** written only for this expert from research item 10, sent the same day they reply, with the page and calendar under them. It is the default in every framework close. F9 is the framework built around the questions, and Closer 2 offers them again.
- Never "book a call." Never "hop on." The booking happens after the reply.
- At least 8 of the 10 frameworks close on the three-questions ask. F10 ends on a soft question instead, and it still carries a short out ("Honest question, and it's fine to skip it.").
- **Every close carries an easy out** from the escape-hatch bank below. "No pitch, nothing hidden" is a terms line, not an out, and never counts as one.
- **Word it fresh.** No two emails to one lead close with the same sentence or the same skeleton (the same opening words and main verb, such as "Reply and I'll send..."), and no out repeats within a lead, in words or in idea. The close and skeleton rule covers the 13 framework closes, the follow-up lines that offer the questions, and both closers. The out-by-idea rule covers the escape hatch in each framework close and the F9 follow-up's out. Follow-up job lines (the honest no-reply admission, yes or no both welcome) follow the job table instead, and the closer opt-outs follow their own bank. The banks are models. The agent rewords them per lead and logs which ones a lead has had.
- The page link in four follow-ups does not spend the reward. The reward is the questions, and the page never carries them.

**Close-variation bank (three-questions reward).** Every live close in the doc is a row here, with the email that shows it. A lead gets each skeleton at most once. Rows 1, 4 and 7 share one skeleton ("Reply and I'll send..."), so a lead gets only one of them. Rows 10 and 11 clash with the F9 follow-up and Closer 2 ("Reply 'send'...", "Reply and they're yours"), so they never run as a framework close.

| # | Phrasing | `Roster false:` form | Shown in |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | "Reply and I'll send the three questions I'd ask you." | "Reply and I'll send the three questions Justin, who hosts it, would ask you." | F1 |
| 2 | "Want the three questions I'd ask you? Just reply." | "Want the three questions Justin, who hosts it, would ask you? Just reply." | F2 |
| 3 | "Hit reply and you'll have the three questions today." | same (no host verb) | F3 |
| 4 | "Reply and I'll send three questions written only for you." | same | spare (skeleton of row 1) |

| 8 | "One reply and the three questions come back the same day." | same (no host verb) | F4 |

**Escape-hatch bank (pair one with every close; never repeat within a lead):**
1. "If it's not for you, no problem."
2. "Totally fine if the answer is no."
3. "Even a 'not for me' helps, so I stop guessing."
4. "If now's a bad time, it can wait."
5. "Yours either way." (only right after a questions close)
6. "No is a fine answer too."
7. "If you'd rather pass, I get it."
8. "Zero pressure on this one."
9. "If you're slammed right now, that's fair."
10. "A one-word no is just as welcome."
11. "If interviews aren't your thing, that's okay."
12. "Happy either way."
13. "It's fine to skip it." (F10 only, folded into "Honest question, and it's fine to skip it.")
14. "If camera's a hard no, I understand." (Alt C only)
15. "And I won't take a no personally." (F9 follow-up only)
16. "No worries if it's not a fit." (F6)
17. "If one show is enough, no harm done." (Alt A, Track B)

Outs are counted by idea as well as by words: no two framework-close outs to one lead (plus the F9 follow-up's out) make the same point in different words. Follow-up job lines follow the job table, not this rule. The examples in this doc use one idea each: not for you (F1), a no is fine (F2), timing (F3), not your thing (F4), passing (F5), fit (F6), busy (F7), pressure (F8), yours either way (F9), skipping (F10), one show is enough, no harm done (Alt A), a one-word no (Alt B, thin leads only), camera (Alt C), not taking it personally (F9 follow-up).

**Opt-out lines (Closer 1 and Closer 2 only; a separate bank so they never echo an out the lead already had):**
- "If this isn't for you, just say so and I'll stop."
- "Rather not? One word back and you won't hear from me again." (reworded from "Not your thing?", which echoed F4's out)
- "If you'd rather I didn't write again, reply 'stop' and that's that."

Spin the chosen opt-out at word level. Never "silence means no." Never imply we'll keep emailing regardless.

**The signature-line system (exact phrasings, each with a home and a limit):**

| Line | Exact phrasing (vary lightly) | Home | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Terms line** | Full: "It isn't a pitch, and nothing is hidden. We just want to connect with real experts." Short: "No pitch, nothing hidden." | F3 and Closer 2 (full) | Short form allowed in any email, once |
| **No-charge line** | "There's no charge." | F3 only | Once per lead. Its own sentence, never fused with the terms line into a list. Nowhere else, Closer 2 included. |
| **Thesis line** | "No matter how good AI gets, it can't replace what a veteran knows." | F2, F10, Alt A | Once per email, only in its homes. At most three of a lead's frameworks. |
| **Wisdom line** | "It's not what you know. It's what you've seen, and what you notice that nobody else does." | F1 | Once per lead. Tie it to the sentence before it ("because it's not what you know...") so it never reads as a stray slogan. |
| **Interview line** | "A 20 to 30 minute interview about what you've learned." | Any | Once per email |
| **Feature line** | Full: "We send it to our email list and feature it on our socials. After that it's yours to share." Short: "It's yours to share." | F6 (full) | Short form elsewhere, once |
| **Room line** | "You'd be in a room with other people who are the best at what they do." | Held: no live home | Not in copy until Open Item 7b is confirmed and real interviews exist, because it implies other guests and adjacent experts watching. F7 no longer uses it. |
| **Credibility line** | "I've taught 300 agency owners, and I was asked to speak at an AI summit." | F8 only | Never anywhere else. First person only when `justin_background` is true. Never mention referral partnerships. |

Two or three signature lines per email, never all. The spine shows up in every email. The lines rotate.

**Follow-up jobs (one per follow-up; the framework blocks carry the `*Job:*` label):**

| Framework | Job | Page link |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | Forgot to mention: one new true detail about the series | yes |
| F2 | The useful one: one true observation about their field | no |
| F3 | Honest no-reply admission: "No reply usually means busy, not no." | no |
| F4 | Yes or no both welcome | yes |
| F5 | Forgot to mention | no |
| F6 | The useful one | no |
| F7 | The practical one: the total time, and that they pick the slot themselves (plus the page link), then a question about their craft. Never a yes-or-no ask (F4 owns that job). | yes |
| F8 | The useful one | no |
| F9 | The plain version: one reply-send line, one out in fresh words (never used elsewhere in the lead, never from the closer opt-out bank), then one craft question. No "answer one here" option, ever. | no |
| F10 | Pure question, soft. Never "would you be open to it." | yes |
| Alt A | The useful one, ending on a question about their craft | no |
| Alt B | Yes or no both welcome | no |
| Alt C | Honest no-reply admission | no |

**Hard rules:**
- Framework emails 85 to 100 words, follow-ups 30 to 50.
- **Reading grade 5 or lower is the target. Grade 7 is the ceiling.** Short words, short sentences, one idea per sentence.
- Exactly one research detail, in the first two lines. "Saw your website" does not count. One detail per email, never reused across a lead's 22 touches.
- **Opener variety:** at most 3 of the 13 relevance lines may start with "Saw", and no two frameworks in a row may open with the same verb. Other ways in: "Your clinic's FAQ explains...", "A patient wrote that...", "Three reviews say...", "Twenty-two years of...".
- One pain per email. End on the reply ask or a question. Never a pitch.
- Plain text. No bold, images, buttons. No links in framework emails.
- **Follow-up links:** the page link (with the lead's ref) appears ONLY in the follow-ups of F1, F4, F7 and F10. Every other follow-up carries no link and ends on a question about their craft. A closer carries one link at most.
- **Follow-ups never open with "following up on"** and never refer to the email by a label nobody would say aloud ("the ring light note"). Each does its own job from the table above.
- No "hope this finds you well," "I wanted to reach out," "I'd love to," "hop on a quick call," "honored," "excited."
- First person. Peer to peer.
- No em-dashes or en-dashes anywhere, subjects included. No exclamation marks.
- No perfectly parallel three-item lists. Vary sentence length hard. Long, short, fragment.
- Every framework email stands alone. Never "as I mentioned" or "my last note." A follow-up references only its own framework's email.
- **Banned words:** price, cost, fee, fees, investment, spend, budget, unlock, 10x, synergy, leverage, innovative, cutting-edge, solution, game-changer, transform, revolutionize, scale your, disrupt, guaranteed, ROI, lead generation, automation, opportunity, passive income, furthermore, moreover, delve, landscape, robust, podcast (about us; we are an interview series), exposure, influencer, content creator, brand, amazing, awesome, excited, honored, reach out, touch base. "AI" only per the claims section.
- **Niche-vocabulary exceptions:** "agency" only inside F8's credibility line ("300 agency owners") and in "not an agency." "Podcast" only about the prospect's own show (Track B), never about us.
- **Money:** nothing about money in either direction. No "free" as a hook, no "no cost." "No charge" appears once per lead, in F3 only. Never promise new business, customers or leads. Allowed: "if somebody watching needs what you do, they'll know where to find you."
- **Never promise outcomes:** no views, no audience size, no "this will get you clients." Never state our list size.
- **Never claim what isn't confirmed:** not "the clips are yours to own," not "experts in nearby fields see it." Both wait on Justin (Open Items).
- **Never fabricate:** no invented guests, past episodes, quotes, results, or numbers. Until real episodes exist, never say "our last guest" or name anyone.

**Spintax (Instantly):**
- **Format:** `{{RANDOM | option one | option two | option three}}`. Double braces are the only braces allowed in upload-ready copy. Single-brace placeholders (`{sender}`, `{page link}`, `{first_name}`) are agent instructions and must never reach a sent email.
- **Word level, not sentence level.** Swap synonyms across a sentence, not one word in a repeated sentence.
- **Every framework's spin set:**
  - subject: `{{RANDOM | a | b | c}}`, 3 or more options, each a complete 1 to 4 word lowercase subject
  - greeting: `{{RANDOM | Hey | Hi}} {Name},`
  - sign-off: `{{RANDOM | {sender} | Thanks, {sender} | Cheers, {sender}}}`
- **Also spun:** the Closer 1 subject, the Closer 2 stock opener ("Last one from me, no hard feelings."), and the opt-out line in each closer. Each closer block carries those options. "Fair enough?" is the required Closer 2 ending and is never spun.
- **Reworded per lead instead of spun:** follow-ups and escape hatches. Every follow-up is written for that lead from its own framework, and the agent rewords each out per lead from the bank, so neither carries a fixed stock line to spin.
- **Not spun:** the researched sentences (relevance, their ninety seconds). They are already unique per lead.
- Every option must pass every rule on its own: length, banned words, dashes, grade. QC reads all options, not only the first.

## DO'S AND DON'TS

**DO:**
- Make them feel seen. The relevance line should make them think "how did they know that about me."
- Lead with what their customers wrote. The review pattern is the reason we're writing, so say it.
- Write their field's version of the ninety seconds in their own vocabulary. A barber's ninety seconds is not a CPA's.
- Ask about what they know, not about their business. The curiosity is the hook.
- Say the terms early when in doubt. "No pitch, nothing hidden" answers the question every expert has before they finish reading.
- Name the reward. The three questions are worth replying for. "More info" is not.
- Give every ask a way out, so saying no costs nothing.
- Keep it short enough to read on a phone between two jobs.

**DON'T:**
- Don't flatter. "You're amazing" is a pitch. "You're the one the other contractors call" is an observation.
- Don't explain AI, the internet, or marketing to them. Name the thing and move on.
- Don't use the word podcast for what we do. Don't promise views, reach, clients or a bigger audience.
- Don't make it about us. One sentence about the series, the rest is about them.
- Don't hint at what we sell. The interview is the whole ask. Paid programs and the referral partnerships work never appear in cold email, follow-ups or closers, F8 included.
- Don't use the "we'll pay you if it's a hit" line. It is parked until the terms are set (see Open Items).
- Don't open two emails in a row the same way, and don't start every email with "Saw."
- Don't open a follow-up with "following up on." Give it its job.
- Don't say the clips are theirs to own, or that experts in nearby fields will see it, until Justin confirms both.
- Don't promise an "answer by email" option. It isn't in the Offer Block.

## NICHE LANGUAGE GUIDE

**Words that sound right:** what you've learned, what you've seen, the stuff nobody writes down, you just know, the call they make when they're stuck, years in, on the record, the real ones, the go-to, the person people ask for by name.

**Words that sound wrong:** content, thought leader, personal brand, guru, influencer, visibility, exposure, platform, audience growth, featured guest opportunity.

**Their word for the people they serve:** use the segment's word (customers, clients, patients, guests, homeowners, owners, members). Never "users" or "consumers."

---

## THE 10-PAIN AMMO BANK (+4 bench pains)

These are the truths of being an expert, written in their language. One per email, never stacked.

1. **The ninety seconds (the signature).** You know in seconds what took twenty years to learn. You see it, hear it, feel it, and you're right. Nobody has ever asked you how you know, and you'd struggle to write it down.
2. **The loud ones.** Somebody with two years in and a ring light is called the expert online in your field. You're too busy doing the actual work to post about it.
3. **Written by something that's never done it.** Search any question in your field and you'll get a confident answer from something that has never touched the job. Customers read it, then come to you with the wrong idea.
4. **The stories nobody wrote down.** The strange jobs, the near misses, the save at the last minute. They live in your head and in your crew's, and nowhere else.
5. **What walks out the door with you.** The judgment you've built doesn't transfer by manual. Apprentices learn it by standing next to you, and there are never enough standing there.
6. **Judged by stars.** Customers boil you down to a rating and a quote. The thing that actually makes you different, your judgment, doesn't fit in a review.
7. **The question you answer fifty times.** You explain the same thing to every new customer. You'd love to say it right, once, and send it to people.
8. **Invited with everyone else.** The "top expert" invites you get went out to everyone in your field. Nothing in them was about you, so you stopped opening them. (F7's pain. It pairs with the true scarcity: only a couple a day, so each one is picked.)
9. **Crazy times.** People starting out in your field are anxious that everything is about to change. A veteran saying what doesn't change would help them more than another article.
10. **The pitch in a costume.** You've had the "we'd love to feature you" email before. It turned out to be a sales pitch. So you ignore them now.

**Bench pains:**
- B1. **Not a camera person.** You'd rather do the job than talk about it on video.
- B2. **The family business.** You learned it from your father or a mentor. Their lessons are in you and nowhere else.
- B3. **The second career.** You came into this from somewhere else, and you see things lifers don't.
- B4. **The people you should know.** The best people in the fields next to yours, the ones who serve your customers before or after you, have never met you. Held: never in copy until Open Item 7b is confirmed, because it only pays off if those experts see the series.

---

## SEGMENT SWAP TABLE

The frameworks stay the same. The nouns and the ninety seconds change. The agent writes the ninety seconds fresh from research, using the example here only as a model of the move. A model is never stated as fact about the lead; hedge it ("I'd bet you can...") unless the reviews say it.

| Segment | Their word for customers | Their ninety seconds (model) | Detail swaps (what to look for) | Skip or swap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Auto and repair | customers | hears the car pull in and knows it's the timing belt | years in the bay, makes they specialize in, a review about the diagnosis | none |
| Home and trades | homeowners | opens the wall and knows what's behind the next one | specialty (old houses, commercial), license years, a review naming the fix | none |
| Personal care | clients | watches you walk in and knows the cut that works with your hair | chair years, a signature technique, a client quote | Alt C often fits |
| Health and wellness | patients or clients | watches you walk across the room and knows where it hurts | specialty, training, a patient story they posted | Claims: never mention outcomes or results |
| Family, pets and learning | families, owners, students | meets the dog for two minutes and knows why it pulls | breed or age specialty, method name, years | none |
| Food and hospitality | guests | tastes the sauce and knows the one thing the line cook skipped | signature dish, origin story, a review about one plate | none |
| Real estate and property | buyers, sellers, owners | walks into a house and knows what it'll sell for | neighborhoods, deal types, years, a post about one deal | none |
| Professional services | clients | reads a P&L for ninety seconds and asks the question others missed | niche clients, credentials, a post or article they wrote | Licensed: never position them as giving advice in the interview |
| Marketing and creative | clients | hears your offer for sixty seconds and knows why the ads aren't working | portfolio piece, niche, a post they wrote | Track B is common here |
| Technology | clients | reads the spec and knows which feature doubles the budget | stack, a project, a post about a failure | Track B is common here |
| Product founders | customers, buyers | knows which buyer at the chain actually decides | the product's origin, a retailer win, the founder's story | none |
| Coaching and consulting | clients | hears a founder describe their week and knows the one hire that fixes it | method, background, a talk or post | Track B is common here |

**Who the real buyer is:** the expert themself. In a firm, the partner or principal who is the named expert, not the marketing person. In a family business, whoever the reviews name.

## RESEARCH — HOW THE AGENT FINDS THE ONE SPECIFIC THING

**The list signal (new in v2): the review pattern.** The list is filtered on it before research starts. Several reviews name the same judgment skill in the customer's own words: found what others missed, knew right away, talked me out of the thing I didn't need, the one other pros call. That pattern is the reason we're writing, so it usually becomes the Gold detail in the lead framework (F1 by default). List & Signals scrapes the reviews, scores them against a phrase set written per segment, and logs the pass rate. A lead without the pattern never reaches research. This is the list-level version of the Gold detail below.

This campaign lives or dies on the relevance line. The goal is one detail that is unique to this person and true of their field, the kind of thing that makes them think "they actually looked." The agent researches every lead before writing a single word.

**Where to look (all of them, in this order):**
1. **Their website.** About page, team page, "our story," services, any blog posts or FAQs they wrote themselves.
2. **Google Business Profile and reviews.** Read at least 20 reviews. Look for the same specific skill named by different customers ("he found what three other shops missed"). Confirm the review pattern the list was filtered on, and note the exact thing found.
3. **LinkedIn.** Years in the field, career path, past roles, posts, articles, recommendations.
4. **Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, YouTube.** Their own posts and videos, especially any where they explain something, show a job, or tell a story.
5. **Podcasts, local news, press, awards.** Anything they've been quoted in, won, or spoken at. (Also the Track B check.)
6. **Licenses, certifications, associations.** State license records, trade association listings, board certifications, years held.
7. **Industry context.** Two minutes on their field: what's changing, what veterans complain about, what newcomers get wrong. This feeds their ninety seconds.

**The specificity test (every detail must pass):** could this sentence be sent to any other business in their category? If yes, it fails.
- **Gold:** their own words or a specific skill named in reviews ("Three different reviews say you found the leak two other plumbers missed."; "Your post about why you stopped doing laminate.") Name the thing that was found. "What two other shops missed" without the thing is weaker.
- **Silver:** a specific fact about them (the specialty, years, the origin story, an award, the shop their father started).
- **Bronze:** city plus category ("a plumber in Tampa"). Bronze never counts on its own.

**The 10-minute rule:** the relevance line says what a smart person would conclude after 10 minutes of looking, not "loved your website."

**Research checklist (all logged per lead, with the source):**
1. **Segment** from the swap table.
2. **First name** of the expert (the person, not the company).
3. **Track:** A (quiet) or B (already talks). Note the channel if B.
4. **Ten details, Gold or Silver,** one for each of the ten framework emails (F1 to F10, or the alternates that replace them), never reused across the lead's touches. One fact per detail: tenure plus a draw radius is two details, not one. If fewer than ten pass the test, see the routing rule below.
5. **Their ninety seconds:** one sentence, in their vocabulary, written from the reviews, posts and industry context.
6. **Their story hooks:** origin, family business, second career, a notable job or save (feeds F5, F9, bench pains).
7. **Their field's "loud ones":** the kind of person called an expert online in their field without the years (feeds F4; categories only, never named).
8. **Adjacent fields:** two or three kinds of businesses that serve their customers before or after them. Logged only. Nothing in live copy uses them until Open Item 7b is confirmed (then they feed the room line and bench pain B4). F7 no longer names adjacent fields.
9. **Camera signals:** photos or video of the expert themself, or none (none routes Alt C higher).
10. **The three questions (the reply reward):** three interview questions written only for them, drawn from items 4 to 6. Logged at research time so the reward goes out the same day as the reply. Each must pass the swap test: if a question could go to another business in their category, rewrite it.
11. **Regulated field check:** health, legal, finance, insurance, real estate licensing. If yes, no outcomes, no advice language, ever.
12. **Sender-truth check:** read the roster flags for the sending inbox.
13. **The list signal:** the review pattern, the reviews that carry it, and their source.

**Routing rule (how many details decides how long the sequence is):**
- **Ten or more passing details:** the full Standard sequence. Ten framework emails, ten follow-ups, two closers (22 touches).
- **Five to nine passing details:** the sequence runs only as many framework emails as there are details, each with its follow-up, then Closer 1 and the Closer 2 for the lead's track. Frameworks without a detail are skipped in back-to-front order of the lead's set order (F10 first, then F8, F6, F7 and so on, so no two frameworks from one bucket land side by side), and F1 and F9 are always kept. The lead framework is never skipped either. Example: seven details in the default order runs F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F7, F9 (16 touches).
- **Two to four passing details:** Alternate B leads and is the only framework email. Then its follow-up, Closer 1 and the thin research Closer 2 (4 touches). It uses one of the details and the field's ninety seconds.
- **Fewer than two passing details:** skip the lead.

Every route reuses nothing. Never send a bracket. Never send a guess. Never invent a detail.

## THE OFFER BLOCK — WHAT'S TRUE (for the agent and the setter, never pasted)

- **The Real Experts Series** interviews people at the top of their field about what they've learned.
- **The call:** about 15 minutes to get to know each other. If it's a fit, a 20 to 30 minute recorded interview right after. In the last few minutes we book a short review call. About 45 minutes total.
- **After:** our team edits the interview and cuts short clips. They see it first. Once they approve, we send it to our email list and feature it on our socials, and they can share it anywhere.
- **The terms:** there's no charge. It isn't a pitch, and nothing is hidden. We just want to connect with real experts.
- **The reply reward (default, every framework close):** the three interview questions written only for them (research item 10), sent the same day they reply. Under them goes the page, experts.truerevenuepartnerships.com/?ref={lead_ref}, which has the video, what happens on the call, and the calendar. The ref carries through to the booking.
- **The free thing:** the same three questions. Theirs whether they do the interview or not. The default reward in every close; F9 is built around them; Closer 2 offers them again.
- **Behind the curtain (never in email, follow-ups or closers):** the referral partnerships work and the paid programs. F8's credibility line says Justin has taught 300 agency owners, never what he taught them. If asked how we make money, the honest answer is in the reply templates.
- **Not true, never said:** audience size, views, past guests, "you'll get clients," "we'll pay you."
- **Not confirmed, never said until Justin confirms:** that the interview and clips are delivered as files they own, and that experts in adjacent fields see it (Open Items 7a and 7b).

---

# FRAMEWORK 1: "The Ninety Seconds"

**Angle:** the signature. Name the thing they found that others missed, then the knowing behind it (their field's ninety seconds, hedged as a guess, never stated as fact). They feel seen. Then the invitation, and a reply for the three questions. The universal opener, and the best email in the doc.

**Pain pairing:** #1 (the ninety seconds).

**Signature lines used:** wisdom line (folded into the offer sentence), interview line, terms line (short).

**Subject line options:** `ninety seconds` | `how you know` | `the intermittent stall` (swap to their field's tell)

**Structure:**

> {relevance: one Gold detail naming the skill a reviewer named, with the source logged}
>
> {pain #1: "I'd bet" their ninety seconds in their own words, hedged; the knowing took years and probably nobody asked how}
>
> {invitation: the Real Experts Series; wisdom line folded in with "because"; interview line; terms short form}
>
> {close: reply for the three questions + easy out}

**Example (auto repair, Akron):**

> Hey Ray,
>
> Three reviews say you found the intermittent stall two other shops missed.
>

>
> Reply and I'll send the three questions I'd ask you. If it's not for you, no problem.
>
> {sender}

*Roster false:* "Reply and I'll send the three questions Justin, who hosts it, would ask you. If it's not for you, no problem."

**Follow-up (reply in thread, 3 days later):**
*Job:* forgot to mention (one new true detail about the series, plus the page link)

    greeting: {{RANDOM | Hey | Hi}} Ray,
    sign-off: {{RANDOM | {sender} | Thanks, {sender} | Cheers, {sender}}}

# FRAMEWORK 2: "Written By Something That's Never Done It"

**Angle:** the thesis. A new owner can ask a machine and get a confident answer from something that has never done the job. They have. That's why the series exists.

**Pain pairing:** #3 (written by something that's never done it).

**Signature lines used:** thesis line, interview line.

**Subject line options:** `never done it` | `the confident answer` | `ask a machine`

**Structure:**

> {relevance: one detail, ideally about a specific thing they did or do}
>
> {pain #3: customers arrive with a confident answer from something that never did the job}
>
> {invitation: the Real Experts Series; the thesis line; interview line}
>
> {close: reply for the three questions + easy out}

**Example (bookkeeping, Phoenix):**

> Hey Dana,
>
> Your bio mentions you started on the floor as a server.
>
> A new owner can ask a machine how to read a P&L and get a confident answer from something that has never sat with a restaurant owner at midnight. You probably have.
>
> That's why I'm doing the Real Experts Series. No matter how good AI gets, it can't replace what a veteran knows. It's a 20 to 30 minute interview about what you've seen.
>
> Want the three questions I'd ask you? Just reply. Totally fine if the answer is no.
>
> {sender}

*Roster false:* "Want the three questions Justin, who hosts it, would ask you? Just reply."

**Follow-up (reply in thread, 3 days later):**
*Job:* the useful one (one true observation about their field)

> Hey Dana, a P&L only tells an owner what already happened. The midnight question is what to do about it, and nobody can look that up. What's the first line you check when the numbers feel off?

**Spin set:**
    subject: {{RANDOM | never done it | the confident answer | ask a machine}}
    greeting: {{RANDOM | Hey | Hi}} Dana,
    sign-off: {{RANDOM | {sender} | Thanks, {sender} | Cheers, {sender}}}

# FRAMEWORK 3: "No Pitch, Nothing Hidden"

**Angle:** terms-led. They've had the "we'd love to feature you" email, and it was a sales pitch. This one says the terms plainly up front. Allowed to stack three signature lines. The only home of "no charge" in the doc.

**Pain pairing:** #10 (the pitch in a costume).

**Signature lines used:** terms line (full), no-charge line (its own sentence), interview line. Three, the most any email carries.

**Subject line options:** `not a pitch` | `nothing hidden` | `the catch`

**Structure:**

> {relevance: one detail}
>
> {pain #10: you've had the "feature you" email that turned out to be a sales pitch}
>
> {invitation: the Real Experts Series; interview line; terms line full; "There's no charge." as its own sentence, once}
>
> {close: reply for the three questions + easy out}

**Example (residential roofing, Charlotte):**

> Hey Mike,
>
> Your site says you still climb every roof yourself before quoting.
>
> You've probably had the "we'd love to feature you" email. Then it turns out to be a sales pitch.
>
> This isn't that. The Real Experts Series is a 20 to 30 minute interview about what you've learned. It isn't a pitch, and nothing is hidden. We just want to connect with real experts. There's no charge.
>
> Hit reply and you'll have the three questions today. If now's a bad time, it can wait.
>
> {sender}

*Roster false:* no swap needed. This example has no first-person host line (the close names the questions, not who asks them). If a writer adds "I'd ask" or "I wrote", it swaps to "Justin, who hosts it, would ask" or "we wrote".

**Follow-up (reply in thread, 3 days later):**
*Job:* honest no-reply admission

> Hey Mike, no reply usually means busy, not no, and a roofer is always busy. The three questions are there whenever you want them. What's the roof that taught you the most?

**Spin set:**
    subject: {{RANDOM | not a pitch | nothing hidden | the catch}}
    greeting: {{RANDOM | Hey | Hi}} Mike,
    sign-off: {{RANDOM | {sender} | Thanks, {sender} | Cheers, {sender}}}

# FRAMEWORK 7: "Two A Day"

**Angle:** structurally true scarcity. The host only records a couple of interviews a day, so each one is picked for the work behind it. The pain is the mass invite: every other "top expert" invite they get went to everyone. This one went to them. Back half. Never names adjacent fields, and never implies who else is in the series, until Open Item 7b is confirmed and real interviews exist.

**Pain pairing:** #8 (invited with everyone else).

**Signature lines used:** interview line, terms line (short).

**Subject line options:** `two a day` | `just a couple` | `picked for this`

**Structure:**

> {relevance: one detail, used as the opener, never "Saw"}
>
> {pain #8: the "top expert" invites they get probably went to everyone in their field, hedged as a guess}
>
> {invitation: the Real Experts Series; only a couple a day, so each one is picked; interview line; terms short}
>
> {close: ask for the questions the host would start with, in their inbox today; out: "If you're slammed right now, that's fair."}

**Rule:** "a couple a day" is true only while the recording schedule holds (Open Item 2). If the schedule changes, this framework's scarcity line changes with it.

**Example (real estate agent, Nashville):**

>
> Your brokerage profile has you selling more East Nashville homes than anyone in your office, six years running.
>
> I'd guess most "top agent" invites you get went to every agent in town.

>
> Ask for the questions I'd start with, and they'll be in your inbox today. If you're slammed right now, that's fair.
>
> {sender}

*Roster false:* swap "I only have room for a couple of Real Experts Series interviews a day" for "Justin, who hosts the Real Experts Series, only has room for a couple of interviews a day", and "the questions I'd start with" for "the questions Justin would start with".

**Follow-up (reply in thread, 3 days later):**
*Job:* the practical one (the total time, and that they pick the slot themselves, plus the page link), then a question about their craft.

> Hey Carla, a short note on time. The whole call takes about 45 minutes, start to end, and you pick the slot here: {page link}. What do new sellers in East Nashville never see coming?

**Spin set:**

# ALTERNATE B: "The One Thing" (thin research)

**When it swaps in:** research found only two to four passing details. Alt B then leads and is the only framework email: Alt B, its follow-up, Closer 1 and the thin research Closer 2 (4 touches). No detail is ever reused. It uses the field's ninety seconds from the swap table, written fresh, plus one passing detail. With five to nine details, Alt B does not run; the sequence is shortened instead (see the routing rule in Research).

**Angle:** the one thing about them we know is enough. The rest is the question.

**Pain pairing:** #1 (the ninety seconds), from the field's model.

> I've got three questions with your name on them, ready when you reply. A one-word no is just as welcome.
>
> {sender}

**Follow-up (reply in thread, 3 days later):**
*Job:* yes or no both welcome

> Hey Beth, either a yes or a no helps me, so don't overthink it. It's a conversation, not a presentation. What do owners get wrong about their dog in the first week?

**Spin set:**
    subject: {{RANDOM | the one thing | a question | how long}}

# FRAMEWORK SELECTION LOGIC

The research decides which framework LEADS. The rest follow by relevance, one bucket at a time, with F7 (scarcity) and F9 (free thing) always in the back half.

| Research finding | Lead framework |
|---|---|
| Gold detail from reviews naming a specific skill (the list signal; most leads) | F1 "The Ninety Seconds" |
| Track B (podcast, channel, newsletter, regular posts) | Alt A "You Already Share It" |
| Family business, a mentor, or an origin story | F5 "What Goes With You" |
| A repeated customer question visible (FAQ, posts, reviews asking the same thing) | F6 "Say It Once" |
| They've visibly turned down paid features, or the field is full of pay-to-play outlets | F3 "No Pitch, Nothing Hidden" |
| They teach, mentor or hire juniors | F10 "Honest Question" (move to front half only here) |
| Five to nine passing details | Lead as usual. The sequence runs only as many framework emails as there are details (routing rule in Research): frameworks without a detail are skipped in the order F10, F8, F6, F7, F5..., F1, F9 and the lead are kept |
| Two to four passing details | Alt B "The One Thing" leads and is the only framework email, then its follow-up and the two closers (thin research Closer 2) |
| Fewer than two passing details | Skip the lead |
| No signal stands out | F1 "The Ninety Seconds" (default) |

**The buckets (one at a time, never two in a row from the same bucket):**
- **Seen:** F1, F4, F8 (their skill, their standing, their judgment)
- **Why it matters:** F2, F5, F10 (the thesis, the legacy, the next generation)
- **What it is:** F3, F6, F9 (the terms, the use, the gift)
- **Picked:** F7 (only a couple a day, so each one is picked)

**Default order:** F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10. Track B: Alt A, F2 dropped (Alt A carries the thesis), then F1, F3 to F10. Alt C replaces F8 (back half) when its signals fire.

**Checks:** F7 and F9 in the back half (frameworks 6 to 10), and Alt C, when it runs, in F8's slot. The thesis line appears in no more than three of a lead's frameworks. F8 runs only per the roster. Once the order is set, check the openers: no two frameworks in a row open with the same verb, and at most 3 start with "Saw."

---

# CAMPAIGN STRUCTURE — THE POLICY (Sept 3, 2026)

1. Each framework is its own custom email.
2. There's a follow-up to it, in the same thread, written for that framework's angle.
3. The next framework is a custom email with one follow-up to it.
4. Every campaign runs all ten frameworks this way, then two more follow-ups at the end.

**In touches:** 10 framework emails + 10 follow-ups + 2 closers = 22 touches per lead, for a lead with ten passing details (one per framework email, never reused).

**Thin research runs shorter, never with a reused or invented detail** (routing rule in Research):
- Five to nine passing details: that many framework emails, each with its follow-up, then the two closers. Frameworks without a detail are skipped in the order F10, F8, F6, F7, F5...; F1, F9 and the lead framework always run. Seven details means 7 + 7 + 2 = 16 touches.
- Two to four passing details: Alt B, its follow-up, Closer 1 and the thin research Closer 2 = 4 touches.
- Fewer than two: the lead is skipped.

In Instantly, a shortened lead is never loaded with blank steps. It goes into a separate campaign whose step count matches its route (for example 16 steps or 4 steps), with the same per-step rules.

**Cadence:** framework email day 0, its follow-up 3 days later, the next framework 3 days after that. A framework every 6 days. About two months per lead.

| Step | What | Thread | Subject |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1, 3, 5 ... 19 | Framework emails, lead first from the selection table | new thread each | its own lowercase subject, spun |
| 2, 4, 6 ... 20 | The follow-up to the framework just sent | reply in that thread | none |
| 21 | Closer 1, the short one | new thread | spun (below) |
| 22 | Closer 2, the breakup, with the three questions offered again | reply in thread | none |

**Closer 1 subject:** `{{RANDOM | last note | a question | still worth asking}}`

**Rules that travel with the policy:**
- Every framework email stands alone. A follow-up references only its own framework's email.
- Follow-ups are 30 to 50 words, one question at the end, each with its own job from the follow-up job table.
- The page link (with the lead's ref) goes only in the follow-ups of F1, F4, F7 and F10. If an alternate replaces one of those frameworks, its follow-up stays link-free. Closers carry one link at most.
- No links in framework emails.
- Any reply pauses the sequence and hands off to the reply templates and the setter.
- The second-agent QC pass checks all 22 touches per lead before inboxes are attached.
- In Instantly: 22 steps, odd steps new emails with their own spun subject, even steps replies in thread.

**The free thing: the three questions, now also the default reward.** Three interview questions written only for this expert, from research items 4 to 6, logged at research time (item 10) so they go out the same day as the reply. Theirs whether they do the interview or not. They are the reward in every framework close, F9 is built around them, and Closer 2 offers them one last time.
